    11	
    12	\section{Proof of Overloading Resolution for Functions}
    13	\seclabel{proof-overloading-resolution}
    14	
    15	This section proves that the overloading rules for
    16	function declarations are sufficient to guarantee no undefined nor
    17	ambiguous call at run time (the case for methods is analogous).
    18	
    19	Consider a static function call $\f(\As)$ at some program point $Z$
    20	and its corresponding dynamic function call $\f(\Xs)$.  Let $\Delta$
    21	be the set of parameter types of function declarations of $\f$ that
    22	are visible at $Z$ and applicable to the dynamic call $\f(\Xs)$.  Let
    23	$\Sigma$ be the set of parameter types of function declarations of
    24	$\f$ that are visible at $Z$ and applicable to the static call
    25	$\f(\As)$.  Moreover, let $\sigma$ be the subset of $\Sigma$ for which
    26	no type in $\Sigma$ is more specific and let $\delta$ be the
    27	subset of $\Delta$ for which no type in $\Delta$ is more
    28	specific:
    29	\[
    30	\begin{array}{lclcll}
    31	\sigma & = & \set{S \in \Sigma & | & \lnot \exists S'\in\Sigma: S' \strictsubtype S & }
    32	\\
    33	\delta & = & \set{D \in \Delta & | & \lnot \exists D'\in\Delta: D' \strictsubtype D & }.
    34	\end{array}
    35	\]
    36	
    37	Below we prove:
    38	\[
    39	\begin{array}{l}
    40	|\Sigma| \neq 0 \ \text{implies} \ |\sigma| = 1, and
    41	\\
    42	|\Sigma| \neq 0 \ \text{implies} \ |\delta| = 1.
    43	\end{array}
    44	\]
    45	Informally, if any declaration is applicable to a static call then there
    46	exists a single most specific declaration that is applicable to the
    47	static call and a single most specific declaration that is applicable
    48	to the corresponding dynamic call.
    49	\\
    50	\begin{lemma}
    51	\label{lem:subset}
    52	$\Sigma \subseteq \Delta$.
    53	\end{lemma}
    54	
    55	\begin{proof}
    56	Notice that $\Xs \Ovrsubtype \As$ by type soundness.
    57	If $\f(\Ps)$ is applicable to
    58	the call $\f(\As)$ then $\As \Ovrsubtype \Ps$.  Notice that $\Xs
    59	\Ovrsubtype \As$ implies $\Xs \Ovrsubtype \Ps$.  Therefore
    60	$\f(\Ps)$ is applicable to the call $\f(\Xs)$.
    61	\end{proof}
    62	
    63	\begin{lemma}
    64	\label{lem:dgesge-second}
    65	If $|\Delta| \ge 1$ then $|\delta| \ge 1$.
    66	Also, if $|\Sigma| \ge 1$ then $|\sigma| \ge 1$.
    67	\end{lemma}
    68	
    69	\begin{proof}
    70	Follows from Lemma \ref{lem:nonempty} where $S$ is the set of all
    71	types, $A$ is $\Delta$ and $\Sigma$ respectively,
    72	and the relation $\strictsubtype$ is acyclic and irreflexive.
    73	\end{proof}
    74	
    75	\begin{lemma}
    76	\label{lem:ge}
    77	If $|\Sigma| \ge 1$ then $|\delta| \ge 1$.
    78	\end{lemma}
    79	
    80	\begin{proof}
    81	Follows from Lemmas \ref{lem:subset} and \ref{lem:dgesge-second}.
    82	\end{proof}
    83	
    84	\begin{lemma}
    85	\label{lem:le}
    86	$|\sigma| \le 1$.  Also, $|\delta| \le 1$.
    87	\end{lemma}
    88	
    89	\begin{proof}
    90	We prove this for $\delta$, but the case for $\sigma$ is identical.
    91	For the purpose of contradiction suppose there are two declarations
    92	$\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ in $\delta$.  Since both $\f(\Ps)$ and
    93	$\f(\Qs)$ are applicable without coercion to the call $\f(\Xs)$ we
    94	have $\Xs \Ovrsubtype \Ps \inter \Qs$.  Therefore it is not the case
    95	that $\Ps \incompatible \Qs$.  By the overloading rules, $\Ps
    96	\neq \Qs$ and either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or there is a declaration
    97	$\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ visible at $Z$.  Since it cannot be the case that
    98	$\Ps \excludes \Qs$ there must exist a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter
    99	\Qs)$ visible at $Z$.  Since $\Ps \inter \Qs \Ovrsubtype \Ps$ and $\Ps
   100	\inter \Qs \Ovrsubtype \Qs$ we know $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ is applicable
   101	without coercion to the call $\f(\Xs)$.  Since $\Ps \neq \Qs$ either
   102	$\Ps \inter \Qs \strictsubtype \Ps$ or $\Ps \inter \Qs \strictsubtype
   103	\Qs$.  Either case contradicts our assumption.
   104	\end{proof}
   105	
   106	\begin{theorem}
   107	\label{thm:overloading-subtyping}
   108	If $|\Sigma| \neq 0$ then $|\sigma| = 1$.  Also, if $|\Sigma| \neq 0$
   109	then $|\delta| = 1$.
   110	\end{theorem}
   111	
   112	\begin{proof}
   113	Follows from Lemmas \ref{lem:dgesge-second}, \ref{lem:ge} and \ref{lem:le}.
   114	\end{proof}
   115	
   116	\begin{theorem}
   117	\label{thm:dynamic-subtype-static}
   118	If $\sigma = \set{S}$ and $\delta = \set{D}$ then $D \Ovrsubtype S$.
   119	\end{theorem}
   120	
   121	\begin{proof}
   122	If the declaration with parameter type $S$ and the declaration with
   123	parameter type $D$ satisfy the Subtype Rule then the theorem is
   124	proved.  Otherwise, by the definition of $\sigma$ we have $\sigma
   125	\subseteq \Sigma$.  Therefore $S \in \Sigma$.  By Lemma
   126	\ref{lem:subset}, $S \in \Delta$.  Notice that $S,D \in \Delta$ implies
   127	$X \Ovrsubtype S$ and $X \Ovrsubtype D$.  Therefore, $S \not \excludes
   128	D$.  By the More Specific Rule for Functions, there must exist a
   129	declaration with parameter type $S \inter D$.  Because $X
   130	\Ovrsubtype (S \inter D)$, $(S \inter D) \in \Delta$.
   131	Notice $(S \inter D) \Ovrsubtype S$ and $(S \inter D) \Ovrsubtype D$.
   132	By the definition of $\delta$, we have $\lnot \exists D'\in\Delta: D'
   133	\strictsubtype D$.  In particular, $(S \inter D) \not \strictsubtype
   134	D$.  Therefore $(S \inter D) = D$.
   135	\end{proof}

   441	Applicable declarations are then
   442	determined by the rules for applicability with coercion for dotted
   443	method calls.
   444	
   445	Similarly, a dotted method declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is
   446	\emph{applicable with coercion} to a dotted method call
   447	$\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$ if it $\Cs_0 \Ovrsubtype \Ps_0$ and $\Cs
   448	\substitutable \Ps$.  Notice that the receiver is compared using the
   449	subtype relation instead of the substitutable relation.  This reflects
   450	the restriction that receivers of dotted methods cannot be
   451	coerced.  However, \KWD{self} parameters of functional methods can be
   452	coerced.  This distinction is consistent with the intuition that
   453	functional methods are rewritten into top-level functions.
   454	
   455	Note that the only difference between applicability and applicability
   456	with coercion is that substitutability is used instead of subtyping
   457	to compare the parameter types of the declarations.
   458	
   459	Also note that the definition of applicability with coercion does not
   460	take keyword parameters or varargs parameters into account.  Such
   461	declarations are conceptually rewritten into numerous declarations
   462	which cannot be called with elided arguments nor with variable number of
   463	arguments (as described in \secref{applicability-with-special-params}).  If
   464	one of the expanded declarations is applicable with coercion to a call,
   465	then the original declaration (with keyword or varargs parameters) is
   466	applicable with coercion to the call.
   467	
   468	
   469	
   470	\section{Coercion Resolution}
   471	\seclabel{resolving-coercion}
   472	For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a
   473	declaration that is applicable without coercion.  If so, the most
   474	specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are
   475	explicitly added to the functional call.  If more than one coercion is
   476	possible then the coercion that yields the most specific type is
   477	chosen.  \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
   478	\chapref{overloaded-declarations} describe overloading rules for the
   479	declarations of coercions and overloaded functionals that guarantee
   480	there exists always a most specific coercion when two or more are possible.
   481	
   482	We first define a notion of more specific types in the presence of coercion.
   483	Recall from \secref{type-relations} that Fortress defines an
   484	\emph{exclusion} relation between types which is denoted by $\excludes$.
   485	
   486	For types $T$ and $U$, we say that $T$ \emph{rejects} $U$,
   487	and write $T \rejects U$, if for all coercions to $T$, the type coerced
   488	from excludes $U$:
   489	\[
   490	T \rejects U \iff \forall A: A \coercedefto T \implies A \excludes U.
   491	\]
   492	Note that $T \rejects U$ implies $U \not\coercesto T$.
   493	
   494	We say that $T$ is \emph{no less specific} than $U$, and write $T
   495	\morespecificeq U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ excludes, can be
   496	coerced to, and rejects $U$:
   497	\[
   498	T \morespecificeq U \iff
   499	T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor
   500	(T \excludes U \logicand T \coercesto U \logicand T \rejects U).
   501	\]
   502	
   503	The $\morespecificeq$ relation is reflexive and antisymmetric but not
   504	necessarily transitive.  It is possible, for example, for
   505	three types, $T$, $U$ and $V$, each excluding the other two,
   506	to have coercions from $T$ to $U$ and from $U$ to $V$.  In
   507	this case, $T \morespecificeq U$ and $U \morespecificeq V$ but
   508	$T \not\morespecificeq V$.
   509	
   510	Notice that if two tuple types have a bijective correspondence
   511	between their element types then the $\morespecificeq$ relationship between
   512	the tuple types is equivalent to applying the $\morespecificeq$
   513	relation elementwise.
   514	
   515	We say that $T$ is \emph{more specific} than $U$, and write $T
   516	\morespecific U$, if $T \morespecificeq U \logicand T \neq U$.
   517	
   518	We extend the definitions of no less specific and more specific to
   519	declarations.  We say that a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
   520	specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecificeq \Qs$.
   521	Similarly, we say that a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
   522	specific} than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps)
   523	\morespecificeq (\Qs_0, \Qs)$.  A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more
   524	specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$.
   525	Similarly, a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than
   526	a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps) \morespecific (\Qs_0,
   527	\Qs)$.
   528	
   529	Now we describe how to determine which coercion is applied to a given
   530	call in terms of rewriting functional calls.  The rewriting is
   531	for pedagogical purposes; implementation techniques may vary.
   532	
   533	Consider a static call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$.  Let $\Sigma$ be
   534	the set of parameter types of functional declarations of $\f$ that are
   535	applicable to the call.
   536	Let $\Sigma'$ be the set of parameter types of
   537	functional declarations of $\f$ that are
   538	applicable with coercion to the call.
   539	If $\Sigma$ is not empty then we use the overloading resolution
   540	described in \secref{resolving-overloading} to determine which
   541	element of $\Sigma$ is called.
   542	If $\Sigma$ is empty but $\Sigma'$ is not, then we rewrite the call as
   543	follows.  Define: \[\mathpzc{C} = \{T \in \Sigma' \mid S \coercedefto T
   544	\logicand \As \Ovrsubtype S\}.\] Let $T \in \mathpzc{C}$ be the most
   545	specific element of $\mathpzc{C}$.  In other words, there does not exist
   546	$T' \in \mathpzc{C}$ such that $T' \morespecific T$.  The restrictions
   547	given in \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
   548	\chapref{overloaded-declarations} guarantee that such a $T$
   549	exists and that it is unique.  The call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$ is
   550	rewritten to \EXP{f(\mathrm{coercion}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(\TYP{A}))} or
   551	\EXP{A_{0}.f(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(A))}
   552	and the declaration with parameter
   553	type $T$ is applied to the call.
   554	
   555	As an example, consider the following definitions:
   556	%trait ZZ32 excludes { ZZ64, ZZ128 } end
   557	%trait ZZ64 excludes { ZZ128 }
   558	%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
   559	%end
   560	%trait ZZ128
   561	%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
   562	%  coerce(z:ZZ64) = ...
   563	%end
   564	%
   565	%f(z:ZZ64) = 1
   566	%f(z:ZZ128) = 2
   567	\begin{Fortress}
   568	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}32 \KWD{excludes} \{\,\mathbb{Z}64, \mathbb{Z}128\,\} \KWD{end}\)\\
   569	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}64 \KWD{excludes} \{\,\mathbb{Z}128\,\}\)\\
   570	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
   571	\(\KWD{end}\)\\
   572	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}128\)\\
   573	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\\
   574	\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
   575	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
   576	\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = 1\)\\
   577	\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}128) = 2\)
   578	\end{Fortress}
   579	Then the call \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}32)} resolves to the
   580	declaration \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}64)} because $\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
   581	\morespecific \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}$, which follows from the facts that
   582	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} excludes \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}, coerces to it, and rejects it:
   583	the one type that coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, excludes
   584	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.
   585	The same facts make the two declarations of \VAR{f} a valid overloading, and the
   586	exclusion of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} by \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} does the same for the two
   587	coercions to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128} (\secref{more-specific-rule}).
   588	\revision{revival-coercion-example}{The Working Draft of February 2011 declared the
   589	three traits with no \KWD{excludes} clause and said that the resolution follows
   590	from the fact that \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.
   591	By the definition above, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} is then not more specific than
   592	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}, and neither the two declarations of \VAR{f} nor the two
   593	coercions to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128} are a valid overloading; both implementations
   594	of the revival refuse the example as the Working Draft wrote it.
   595	The clauses added are spelled as \library\ spell those of their integer types,
   596	each trait excluding the wider ones.}
   597	
   598	Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is
   599	statically chosen for a call, this coercion is conceptually inserted
   600	into the call.
   601	This means that the statically chosen coercion is applied at run time.
   602	
   603	For example, in the following program:
   604	%trait A
   605	%  coerce(c:C) = ...
   606	%end
   607	%trait B excludes A end
   608	%trait C end
   609	%object D extends {B,C} end
   610	%
   611	%f(a:A) = 3
   612	%f(b:B) = 4
   613	%
   614	%c : C = D
   615	%f(c)
   616	\begin{Fortress}
   617	\(\KWD{trait} A\)\\
   618	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(c\COLONOP{}C) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
   619	\(\KWD{end}\)\\
   620	\(\KWD{trait} B \KWD{excludes} A \KWD{end}\)\\
   621	\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{end}\)\\
   622	\(\KWD{object} D \KWD{extends} \{B,C\} \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
   623	\(f(a\COLONOP{}A) = 3\)\\
   624	\(f(b\COLONOP{}B) = 4\)\\[4pt]
   625	\(c \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} C = D\)\\
   626	\(f(c)\)
   627	\end{Fortress}
   628	the call to \EXP{f(C)} resolves to the declaration
   629	%\EXP{f(a\COLONOP{}A)}
   630	\EXP{f(A)} despite the fact that the declaration
   631	%\EXP{f(b\COLONOP{}B)}
   632	\EXP{f(B)} is
   633	%dynamically directly
   634	applicable to the dynamic call \EXP{f(D)} and does not require
   635	coercion.
   636	
   637	
   638	
   639	
   640	\section{Restrictions on Coercion Declarations}

20	parameterized with \emph{static parameters}.
    21	Static parameters are \emph{static variables} listed in white
    22	square brackets \EXP{\llbracket} and \EXP{\rrbracket}
    23	immediately after the name of a trait, object, or functional and
    24	they are in scope of the entire body of the declaration.
    25	Static parameters may be instantiated with static expressions discussed in
    26	\secref{static-expr}.
    27	In this chapter, we describe the forms that
    28	these static parameters can take.
    29	
    30	\begin{Grammar}
    31	\emph{StaticParams} &::=&
    32	\bTPl \emph{StaticParamList}\bTPr\\
    33	\emph{StaticParamList} &::=& \emph{StaticParam}(\EXP{,} \emph{StaticParam})$^*$\\
    34	\end{Grammar}
    35	
    36	\section{Type Parameters}
    37	\seclabel{type-param}
    38	
    39	\begin{Grammar}
    40	\emph{StaticParam} &::=&
    41	\emph{Id} \option{\emph{Extends}} \options{\KWD{absorbs} \KWD{unit}} \\
    42	\end{Grammar}
    43	
    44	Static parameters may include one or more type parameters.
    45	Syntactically, a type parameter consists of an identifier followed by an
    46	optional \KWD{extends} clause, followed by an optional
    47	``\EXP{\KWD{absorbs}\;\;\KWD{unit}}'' clause (described in
    48	\secref{absorbing-units}).
    49	If a type parameter does not have an \KWD{extends} clause, it has an
    50	implicit ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}'' clause.
    51	
    52	
    53	Type parameters are instantiated with types such as trait types, tuple types,
    54	and arrow types (See \chapref{types} for a discussion of Fortress
    55	types).  We use the term \emph{naked type variable} to refer to an
    56	occurrence of a type variable as a stand-alone type (rather than as
    57	a parameter to another type).  Type parameters can appear in any context
    58	that an ordinary type can appear, except that a naked type variable must not
    59	appear in the \KWD{extends} clause of a trait or object declaration,
    60	nor in the \KWD{throws} clause of a functional or object declaration,
    61	nor as the type of a \KWD{wrapped} field (discussed in \secref{fields}).
    62	
    63	
    64	Here is a parameterized trait \TYP{List}:
    65	\input{\home/basic/examples/StatParam.Type.tex}
    66	
    67	
    68	\section{Nat and Int Parameters}
    69	\seclabel{natparams}
    70	
    71	\begin{Grammar}
    72	\emph{StaticParam} &::=& \KWD{nat} \emph{Id} \\
    73	&$|$& \KWD{int} \emph{Id} \\
    74	\end{Grammar}
    75	
    76	Static parameters may include one or more
    77	\KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters.
    78	Syntactically, a \KWD{nat} parameter consists of
    79	\KWD{nat} followed by an identifier.
    80	An \KWD{int} parameter consists of
    81	\KWD{int} followed by an identifier.
    82	These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values.
    83	A \KWD{nat} parameter may be used to instantiate other
    84	\KWD{nat} parameters, or to appear in any context that a
    85	variable of type \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can appear,
    86	except that it cannot be assigned to.
    87	An \KWD{int} parameter may be used to instantiate other
    88	\KWD{int} parameters, or to appear in any context that a
    89	variable of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} can appear,
    90	except that it cannot be assigned to.
    91	
    92	
    93	
    94	For example, the following function \VAR{makeVector}:
    95	\input{\home/basic/examples/StatParam.Nat.tex}
    96	declares a \KWD{nat} parameter \EXP{s_{0}}, which appears in both the parameter
    97	type and return type of \VAR{makeVector}.

   568	\section{Intersection and Union Types}
   569	\seclabel{internal-types}
   570	
   571	For every finite set of types, there is a type denoting a unique
   572	\emph{intersection} of those types.
   573	The intersection of a set of types $S$ is a subtype of every type $T \in S$
   574	and of the intersection of every subset of $S$.
   575	There is also a type denoting a unique \emph{union}
   576	of those types. The union of a set of types $S$ is a supertype of every
   577	type $T \in S$ and of the union of every subset of $S$.
   578	Neither intersection types nor union types are first-class types;
   579	they are used solely for type inference (as described in
   580	  \chapref{type-inference}) and
   581	they cannot be expressed directly in programs.
   582	
   583	The intersection of a set of types $S$ is equal to a named type $U$ when
   584	any subtype of every type $T \in S$ and of the intersection of every
   585	subset of $S$ is a subtype of $U$.
   586	Similarly, the union of a set of types $S$ is equal to a named type $U$ when
   587	any supertype of every type $T \in S$ and of the union of every
   588	subset of $S$ is a supertype of $U$.
   589	For example:
   590	%trait S comprises {U,V} end
   591	%trait T comprises {V,W} end
   592	%trait U extends S excludes W end
   593	%trait V extends {S,T} end
   594	%trait W extends T end
   595	\begin{Fortress}
   596	\(\KWD{trait} S \KWD{comprises} \{U,V\} \KWD{end}\)\\
   597	\(\KWD{trait} T \KWD{comprises} \{V,W\} \KWD{end}\)\\
   598	\(\KWD{trait} U \KWD{extends} S \KWD{excludes} W \KWD{end}\)\\
   599	\(\KWD{trait} V \KWD{extends} \{S,T\} \KWD{end}\)\\
   600	\(\KWD{trait} W \KWD{extends} T \KWD{end}\)
   601	\end{Fortress}
   602	because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
   603	clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of
   604	$V$.  Thus, $V = S \inter T$.
   605	
   606	
   607	Intersection types (denoted by $\inter$) possess the following properties:
   608	\begin{itemize}
   609	\item Commutativity: $T \inter U = U \inter T$.
   610	\item Associativity: $S \inter (T \inter U) = (S \inter T) \inter U$.
   611	\item Subsumption: If $S \Ovrsubtype T$ then $S \inter T = S$.
   612	\item Preservation of shared subtypes: If $T \Ovrsubtype S$ and $T \Ovrsubtype U$ then $T \Ovrsubtype S \inter U$.
   613	\item Preservation of supertype: If $S \Ovrsubtype T$ then $\forall U.~S \inter U \Ovrsubtype T$.

   624	\item Preservation of subtype: If $T \Ovrsubtype S$ then $\forall U.~T \Ovrsubtype S \uni U$.

12	\chapter{Type Inference}
    13	\chaplabel{type-inference}
    14	
    15	A call of a function, a method or an operator whose declaration has static
    16	parameters, or of the constructor of an object that has static parameters,
    17	need not write its static arguments, and most calls do not
    18	(\secref{idn-ref}, \secref{dotted-method-calls}).
    19	The static arguments of a call that does not write them are inferred
    20	statically.
    21	This chapter describes that inference for type parameters (\secref{type-param})
    22	and for \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters (\secref{natparams}); the inference
    23	of the static arguments of other kinds of static parameter, and the inference
    24	over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
    25	(\secref{type-inference-components}), are not yet described.
    26	\revision{revival-inference}{The Working Draft of February 2011 left this
    27	chapter a heading and two draft notes, the second of which is kept at its end,
    28	although \chapref{multiple-dispatch}, \secref{idn-ref} and
    29	\secref{dotted-method-calls} cite it.
    30	The rule this chapter states is the one the revival decided on 26, 27 and
    31	28~September 2026 and built into the compiled type checker with this text; the
    32	Working Draft had no counterpart to the rule for a numeral whose conversions tie
    33	(\secref{numeral-default}).
    34	It assumes that a type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause is
    35	bounded by \TYP{Any}, as \library\ and the interpreter take it, where
    36	\secref{type-param} says \TYP{Object}, as the compiled path still takes it for
    37	a program's own declarations (row~412 of the revival's gap ledger).
    38	\chapref{multiple-dispatch} still says that static parameters are inferred
    39	before the applicability of a declaration is checked and before declarations
    40	are compared (\secref{functional-applicability},
    41	\secref{dotted-method-applicability}, \secref{resolving-overloading}), where
    42	this chapter chooses a declaration first.
    43	Those sentences, the implicit bound of \secref{type-param}, and the rule of
    44	\chapref{overloaded-declarations} that a functional whose single parameter has
    45	as its type a naked type parameter of bound \TYP{Any} cannot be overloaded,
    46	which under that bound would forbid overloading any functional whose single
    47	parameter's type is a type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause,
    48	are to be revised together, in the revision of the overloading chapters that
    49	the revival decided on 26~September 2026.
    50	The team's later Types chapter gives the coercion relation and the valid
    51	instantiations of a quantified type, and says nothing of inference.}
    52	
    53	\section{The Static Arguments of a Call}
    54	\seclabel{static-arg-inference}
    55	
    56	The static arguments of a call that does not write them are found in two
    57	steps: the declaration that the call invokes is chosen first, and it is
    58	instantiated second.
    59	
    60	\emph{Choice.}
    61	The declaration is chosen as \secref{resolving-coercion} describes.
    62	A declaration with static parameters is applicable to a call, without or with
    63	coercion, if some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their bounds is
    64	applicable to the call.
    65	Declarations are compared on the parameter types they declare, a declaration
    66	with static parameters on its parameter types taken over every instance that
    67	its bounds allow, and not on an instance inferred for the call.
    68	So a coercion is applied only to make a call possible: it never changes which
    69	declaration is chosen when one is applicable to the call without it.
    70	
    71	\emph{Instantiation.}
    72	The static arguments of the chosen declaration are then inferred, and with them
    73	the instance of the declaration that the call invokes:
    74	\begin{itemize}
    75	\item A type parameter, or a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter, that the
    76	declared type of a parameter mentions other than as the whole type, as
    77	\EXP{b\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} mentions \VAR{T}, is fixed by
    78	the argument at that position, whose type must be a subtype of the parameter
    79	type of the instance.
    80	\item Where the call has an expected type (below), a type parameter that the
    81	declared return type mentions other than as the whole type is fixed by the
    82	expected type as well.
    83	\item A type parameter that is the whole declared type of one or more
    84	parameters, as \VAR{T} is of \EXP{x\COLON{}T}, and that is not fixed as above,
    85	takes, among the types of the arguments at those positions and the types to
    86	which they can be coerced, the narrowest under $\morespecificeq$
    87	(\secref{resolving-coercion}) that every one of those arguments is
    88	substitutable for (\secref{applicability-with-coercion}) and that the bounds of
    89	the type parameter permit.
    90	For number arguments this is the narrowest type into which every one of them
    91	converts: \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and a
    92	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and also for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and an
    93	\EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though neither of them is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
    94	(\secref{basic-integers}).
    95	Where there is no such narrowest type, and the rule for numerals
    96	(\secref{numeral-default}) does not settle the tie, the type parameter takes
    97	the union of the types of those arguments (\secref{internal-types}), if its
    98	bounds permit that, and none of those arguments is converted.
    99	\item Every argument is then admitted against the corresponding parameter type
   100	of the instance by substitutability: an argument whose type is a subtype of it
   101	is passed as it is, and any other argument is coerced to it
   102	(\secref{coercion}), as an argument is coerced to the declared type of a
   103	parameter of a declaration without static parameters.
   104	\end{itemize}
   105	The coercions that the instance needs are inserted into the call statically,
   106	as is any coercion that \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses.
   107	
   108	\emph{The expected type.}
   109	A call has an expected type in these contexts: as the right-hand side of a
   110	variable or field declaration that declares its type, that type; as the
   111	right-hand side of an assignment to a variable whose type is declared, that
   112	type; as the body of a functional that declares its return type, that type;
   113	as the last expression of a block that has an expected type, where no local
   114	declaration precedes it in the block, the block's expected type; and as a
   115	branch of an \KWD{if} expression with an \KWD{else} clause that has an
   116	expected type, the expected type of the \KWD{if} expression.
   117	The expected type is used whether the call is written by tight juxtaposition,
   118	as \EXP{f(x)} (\secref{juxtameaning}), or as a method invocation or an operator
   119	application.
   120	The return type of the instance that the steps above find must be a subtype of
   121	the expected type.
   122	If they find no such instance, the static arguments are inferred again without
   123	the expected type, and the call is accepted only if the return type of the instance
   124	then found is a subtype of the expected type or can be coerced to it; in the
   125	second case the result of the call is coerced to the expected type
   126	(\secref{coercion}).
   127	So, for the declarations
   128	\EXP{\VAR{wrap}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
   129	and \EXP{\VAR{id}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T},
   130	the variable declaration \EXP{a\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket = \VAR{wrap}(3)}
   131	instantiates \VAR{wrap} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, which the expected type fixes,
   132	and coerces the numeral, while \EXP{b\COLON\mathbb{Z}64 = \VAR{id}(3)}
   133	instantiates \VAR{id} at the numeral's own type (\secref{literals}) and coerces
   134	the result.
   135	
   136	\emph{Dispatch.}
   137	The call, with the coercions of its instance inserted, dispatches at run time
   138	as \secref{resolving-overloading} describes, by subtyping and without further
   139	coercion, to the most specific declaration applicable to the converted values.
   140	
   141	For example, of the declarations
   142	\EXP{\VAR{op}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Number}\rrbracket(a\COLON{}T, b\COLON{}T)}
   143	and \EXP{\VAR{op}(a\COLON\TYP{Any}, b\COLON\TYP{Any})}, the call
   144	\EXP{\VAR{op}(z, w)}, where \VAR{z} has type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \VAR{w} has
   145	type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, chooses the first, which is applicable without
   146	coercion, since its instance at \TYP{Number} is, and is more specific than the
   147	second; the first is instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \VAR{z} is coerced,
   148	and the converted call runs that instance.
   149	\revision{revival-inference}{The interpreter has no static types and applies
   150	the same rule at dispatch, from the run-time types of the arguments: it infers
   151	the static arguments of a declaration with static parameters with coercion,
   152	and instantiates the declaration that its dispatch chooses by the rule for a
   153	type parameter that is a parameter's whole type.
   154	So where the declared type of a variable is wider than the type of its value,
   155	or an argument's static type is \TYP{Any}, it may run a declaration at a
   156	narrower instance than the compiled path, which instantiates it at the static
   157	types.
   158	It does not yet fix a type parameter by the expected type, compare
   159	declarations with static parameters on the parameter types they declare, nor
   160	dispatch a converted call again.}
   161	
   162	\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
   163	\seclabel{numeral-default}
   164	
   165	A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
   166	number types (\secref{literals}).
   167	Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
   168	$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
   169	taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
   170	a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
   171	value does not fit in the narrower type.
   172	This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
   173	to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
   174	and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
   175	So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
   176	\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
   177	type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
   178	\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
   179	instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
   180	values.
   181	
   182	The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
   183	Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
   184	call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
   185	is a static error.
   186	
   187	This chapter does not yet describe:
   188	\begin{itemize}
   189	\item the static arguments of a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator
   190	parameter (\secref{boolparams}, \secref{dimunitparams}, \secref{opr-ident});
   191	\item a static parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes,
   192	such as a type parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole type,
   193	or the element type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine
   194	(\secref{reduction-expr}); whether inference may give such a parameter
   195	\TYP{BottomType}, which programmers must not write (\secref{bottom-type}), is
   196	left open;
   197	\item whether an argument whose declared parameter type mentions a static
   198	parameter inside another type may be converted where only a conversion of its
   199	elements would satisfy the bounds of the parameter; under the rule above such
   200	an argument fixes the parameter by subtyping and is not converted;
   201	\item an expected type in any context other than those listed above, such as
   202	an argument of another call, an expression that a local declaration precedes in
   203	a block, an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, a \KWD{typecase}
   204	expression, the body of a \KWD{for} loop, or a call written by loose
   205	juxtaposition, as \EXP{f\;x};
   206	\item the static arguments of an object with static parameters that is named
   207	without a call, which a program writes (\secref{where-clauses});
   208	\item the inference over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
   209	(\secref{type-inference-components}).
   210	\end{itemize}
   211	\revision{revival-inference}{For a type parameter that only the return type
   212	mentions and that the expected type does not fix, the compiled type checker binds the parameter to \TYP{BottomType},
   213	except that it refuses a call that has no expected type when the parameter is
   214	declared \EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}; the interpreter erases such a parameter of a function
   215	to \TYP{BottomType}, and leaves a generic method's uninstantiated (rows~21, 424, 425 and~447 of the revival's gap ledger).
   216	Whether inference may do so is the team's question, kept in the draft note
   217	below.
   218	Neither implementation infers a \KWD{bool} parameter yet: the compiled type
   219	checker refuses by name to infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit}
   220	parameter, and the interpreter does not unify a \KWD{bool} one (rows~21
   221	and~307 of the revival's gap ledger).
   222	The example of \secref{boolparams}, a coercion whose \KWD{bool} parameter only
   223	its parameter type mentions, can be applied only if its argument fixes that
   224	parameter.}
   225	
   226	\note{ \begin{itemize}
   227	 \item
   228	 There seems to be a circular dependency between inference and juxtaposition
   229	 disambiguation -- you have to know if the subexpressions have arrow types
   230	 to disambiguate, but you can't do that without using inference, which
   231	 requires knowing how the variable of unknown type is used.
   232	\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the spec'' on 06/05/07)
   233	\item Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers
   234	\TYP{BottomType}s for static parameters?
   235	 \end{itemize}
   236	}

12	\chapter{Changes Since Fortress 1.0 Specifications}
    13	\applabel{spec-changes}
    14	
    15	\note{Changes Since
    16	http://projectfortress.sun.com/Projects/Community/changeset/1444}
    17	
    18	\section{Changes Made by the 2026 Revival to the Working Draft}
    19	\seclabel{revival-changes}
    20	\sloppy
    21	
    22	This section lists the changes made to this working draft by the 2026
    23	revival of the Fortress project (\url{https://github.com/palimondo/fortress}).
    24	The revival works to finish what the designers intended, judged by this
    25	working draft, and changes the text only where a decision it has taken for
    26	the implementation would otherwise leave the text and the implementation in
    27	open disagreement.
    28	Each changed passage carries a box headed
    29	``Revised by the 2026 revival'' that points to its entry here.
    30	
    31	Each entry gives the affected sections, the change, its rationale, its
    32	effect, the original text, and what reversing to the alternative not taken
    33	would require.
    34	The original text is that of the \emph{Working Draft of February 2011},
    35	the unrevised copy of this document kept in the revival's repository under
    36	the directory \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/}, cited by path and line
    37	there.
    38	The directory's name is misleading: its sources are the working draft of
    39	2~February 2011, and only the file \nolinkurl{fortress.1.0.pdf} in it is the
    40	Fortress~1.0 release.
    41	The full reasoning behind every entry, with each original passage and each
    42	new one, is in the revival's decision records,
    43	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md}
    44	and, for the number chapters,
    45	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md},
    46	in the same repository.
    47	
    48	Every change below follows from one decision of the revival, taken on
    49	24~September 2026 and called \emph{route~A}: the compiled type checker keeps
    50	the type group's rule that no type is a subtype of two different
    51	instantiations of one parameterized trait, a rule this working draft never
    52	stated, and the library's numeric types are reorganized so that they
    53	satisfy it.
    54	The revision of the number chapters (\secref{revival-numbers} to
    55	\secref{revival-reductions}) also carries out three decisions of
    56	26~September 2026 that follow from route~A: on the refined number types, on
    57	conversions between number types, and on sums and products.
    58	The alternative not taken, \emph{route~C}, is described once, in
    59	\secref{revival-routec}.
    60	
    61	\subsection{Instantiation exclusion}
    62	\seclabel{revival-rule}
    63	
    64	\begin{description}
    65	\item[Affected sections] \secref{trait-types}; \secref{trait-decls}.
    66	\item[Change] A property of the exclusion relation is added:
    67	two instantiations of the same parameterized trait exclude each other
    68	unless every static argument other than an operator argument is the same.
    69	The rule it imposes on declarations is added beside the example of
    70	\TYP{InclusiveMolecule}: a trait or object may not extend two such
    71	instantiations, directly or through its supertraits.
    72	\item[Rationale] Without the rule a value may belong to two instantiations
    73	of one parameterized trait, and code specialised for one of them can be
    74	chosen for a caller that was promised the other; with the rule relaxed, the
    75	compiled implementation accepts such a program and fails at run time.
    76	The type group adopted the rule as \emph{multiple instantiation exclusion}
    77	(Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type
    78	Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and
    79	Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011), and the compiled type checker has
    80	enforced it since 2010.
    81	The team's later, unfinished Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) states it in
    82	the two parts used here, under the name \emph{instantiation exclusion}.
    83	Operator arguments do not count: an operator argument only names the
    84	operator a subtrait inherits (\secref{opr-ident}), neither implementation
    85	distinguishes instantiations by it at run time, and the algebra of the
    86	library chapters depends on types that are several instantiations of one
    87	trait differing only in operator arguments.
    88	\KWD{nat}, \KWD{int} and \KWD{bool} arguments count: they are values at
    89	run time (\secref{natparams}, \secref{boolparams}).
    90	\item[Effect] Programs in which a type is a subtype of two instantiations
    91	of one parameterized trait that differ in any other static argument are no
    92	longer valid. The compiled type checker refuses them where the arguments
    93	that differ are types, or numerals given as \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
    94	arguments (row~402 of the revival's gap ledger). It does not yet refuse
    95	them where those arguments are \KWD{bool} arguments, though it accepts boolean parameters written out (row~406),
    96	or where one of them is a static parameter of the trait or object that extends both (row~414).
    97	The interpreter does not check the rule.
    98	The number chapters are revised to the reorganized numeric types
    99	(\secref{revival-numbers}).
   100	\item[Original text] The Working Draft of February 2011 states no such
   101	property; its relations are ``the smallest ones that satisfy all the
   102	properties given in those sections (and this one)''
   103	(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex}, lines
   104	185--189), and the properties it gives for trait types are these (lines
   105	212--216):
   106	\begin{quote}
   107	A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
   108	in which case the defined trait type
   109	excludes every type that appears in that clause.
   110	Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
   111	and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.
   112	\end{quote}
   113	Its rule on declarations is only that of exclusive traits,
   114	``no trait can extend them both''
   115	(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, lines 218--222).
   116	\item[Route C] Replaces this rule by the rule of \secref{revival-routec}.
   117	\end{description}
   118	
   119	\subsection{Where-clause variables in extends clauses}
   120	\seclabel{revival-where}

1029	\subsection{Initializing an array from a function}
  1030	\seclabel{revival-tabulate}
  1031	
  1032	\begin{description}
  1033	\item[Affected section] \secref{arrays}.
  1034	\item[Change] In \figref{arrayFactories}, the method that calls a function at
  1035	each index and initializes the corresponding element with the result is named
  1036	\VAR{tabulate}; \VAR{fill} keeps the method that initializes every element with
  1037	one value.
  1038	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
  1039	it on 26~September 2026.
  1040	The library declares the element type \VAR{E} of an array without a bound and
  1041	instantiates it at tuple types, which the implicit bound \TYP{Object} of
  1042	\secref{type-param} excludes; the interpreter reads such a parameter as bounded
  1043	by \TYP{Any}, and so does the compiled type checker when it checks the library.
  1044	\VAR{E} may then be \TYP{Any} or a function type, and a function passed to
  1045	\VAR{fill} is a value of type \VAR{E} as well as a function from \VAR{I} to
  1046	\VAR{E}: both declarations apply to the call and neither is more specific, which
  1047	the overloading rules forbid (\secref{incompatibility-rule}).
  1048	The compiled type checker refuses the pair; the interpreter chose between the two
  1049	by the argument's run-time type, so that on an array of element type \TYP{Any} a
  1050	function meant as the value was called at each index instead of being stored.
  1051	Where the library derived a second name, it gave it to a form that takes a
  1052	function (\VAR{ivmap} beside \VAR{map}); most languages that have both operations
  1053	name them differently, keeping \VAR{fill} for the value; and \VAR{tabulate} is
  1054	Scala's name for the other.
  1055	\item[Effect] A program initializes an array from a function with
  1056	\VAR{tabulate}. A call of \VAR{fill} with a function stores the function, on an
  1057	array whose element type admits it. The library's factories that build an array
  1058	from a function are renamed with the method; this specification does not list
  1059	them.
  1060	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/parallelism-locality/arrays-distributed.tex},
  1061	line 55, a row of the lower table of the figure:
  1062	\begin{quote}
  1063	\begin{tabular}{|m{2.0in}|m{3.4in}|}
  1064	\hline
  1065	\EXP{\VAR{a}.\VAR{fill}(f\COLONOP{}I\rightarrow{}E)} & {Calls \VAR{f} at each index and initializes the corresponding element with the result of the call.} \\
  1066	\hline
  1067	\end{tabular}
  1068	\end{quote}
  1069	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
  1070	\end{description}
  1071	
  1072	\subsection{The integer type of a range}
  1249	\subsection{The traits that extend a closed trait}
  1250	\seclabel{revival-comprises}
  1251	
  1252	\begin{description}
  1253	\item[Affected sections] \secref{trait-decls}.
  1254	\item[Change] The first sentence of a draft note in \secref{trait-decls},
  1255	which said that the traits listed in a \KWD{comprises} clause are exactly
  1256	the traits that immediately extend the declared trait and that they must
  1257	explicitly extend it, is replaced by normative text: every listed type
  1258	extends the declared trait \VAR{T}, and every value of type \VAR{T} is a
  1259	value of one of the listed types; a listed type may be an instantiation of
  1260	a parameterized trait whose static arguments contain no static variable
  1261	other than the static parameters of \VAR{T}; and a trait or object that explicitly extends
  1262	\VAR{T} is a subtype of a listed type, or a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
  1263	clause of its own each of whose listed types meets the same requirement, or
  1264	a trait with static parameters that at least one trait or object extends
  1265	and every trait or object extending it is a subtype of a listed type.
  1266	The note's second sentence, on a clause that includes ``\EXP{\ldots}'', is
  1267	kept in its note, and the example of \TYP{Molecule} is unchanged.
  1268	The new text answers the third question of Victor Luchangco's draft note
  1269	on trait identifiers earlier in the section, whether an instantiation of a
  1270	parameterized trait may be listed: it may.
  1271	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival
  1272	decided it on 28~September 2026.
  1273	The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) reads a \KWD{comprises}
  1274	clause as coverage: the clause ``specifies a set of types and generic types
  1275	determined by the generic type of the declaration'', and an instantiation of
  1276	the declared generic type ``is covered by the union of the types in this set
  1277	and the corresponding instantiations of the generic type in this set'', one
  1278	generic type $G$ determining another $G'$ ``if every parameter of $G'$ is a
  1279	parameter of $G$''
  1280	(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
  1281	277--283 and 384--390, in the revival's repository).
  1282	Welterweight Fortress, the calculus of the type group's paper of 2012
  1283	(Chase, Hilburn, Luchangco, Naden, Ryu, Steele, and Tristan, ``Dynamic
  1284	Dispatch and Type Inference Semipredicates''), reads it at the level of
  1285	values: ``no value can belong to the trait unless it also belongs to one of
  1286	the comprised types''; its rule for a trait declaration asks nothing of the
  1287	traits that extend a trait with such a clause
  1288	(\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick}, lines 21--22;
  1289	\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-wellformeddecls.tick}, lines 38--62).
  1290	The draft note restated the rule of the compiled type checker of 2009,
  1291	under which \library\ could not close their marker of the integer types as
  1292	the team meant to: \TYP{AnyIntegral} lists the five integer types, and the
  1293	parameterized trait \EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}, which each
  1294	of them extends at itself, stands between them unlisted, as the team's
  1295	comment on the declaration records (``not yet: comprises
  1296	\EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket} where
  1297	\EXP{\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}'', \nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi},
  1298	line 434).
  1299	\TYP{Integral} has a static parameter that \TYP{AnyIntegral} does not have,
  1300	so it can be listed only at particular static arguments, and every value of it is a value of one of the five.
  1301	The full reasoning is in
  1302	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md}
  1303	in the revival's repository.
  1304	\item[Effect] The compiled type checker accepts the declaration of
  1305	\TYP{AnyIntegral} in \library\ as written
  1306	(\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi}, lines 433--436).
  1307	No example of this specification changes: \TYP{ExclusiveMolecule}, which
  1308	has no static parameters, is still not allowed.
  1309	The compiled type checker enforces the requirement on a trait with static
  1310	parameters over the declarations it sees: a trait or object declared in
  1311	another component, below such a trait and a subtype of no listed type, is
  1312	not refused (row~487 of the revival's gap ledger). It compares the declarations it sees by their names: for a parameterized \VAR{T} its verdict can depend on how an extender spells its static parameters, and a trait or object that extends a trait of the same simple name in another API counts as an extender (rows~489 and~490).
  1313	The interpreter does not check \KWD{comprises} clauses.
  1314	The passages that read a \KWD{comprises} clause at the level of types, the
  1315	intersection of two traits with such clauses (\secref{internal-types},
  1316	\secref{more-specific-rule}) and the definitions an abstract function
  1317	declaration requires (\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}), are not
  1318	revised; whether they are to be restated at the level of values is not
  1319	settled.
  1320	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex},
  1321	lines 230--241, a draft note:
  1322	\begin{quote}
  1323	If a trait declaration of \VAR{T} includes a \KWD{comprises} clause
  1324	then the traits listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause
  1325	are exactly the traits that immediately extend \VAR{T}
  1326	and they must explicitly extend \VAR{T}
  1327	(i.e., list \VAR{T} in their \KWD{extends} clause).
  1328	If the \KWD{comprises} clause of a trait \VAR{T} includes ``\EXP{\ldots}''
  1329	(and must therefore be in an API),
  1330	then in a component exporting the enclosing API,
  1331	other traits may explicitly extend \VAR{T},
  1332	but these traits may not be declared or imported by the API
  1333	(see \secref{apis}).
  1334	\end{quote}
  1335	Its second sentence is kept, in its note.
  1336	\item[Route C] The same under route~C, under which the self-typed traits
  1337	carry \KWD{comprises} clauses of their own (\secref{revival-routec}): a
  1338	parameterized trait between a closed trait and its listed types then meets
  1339	the requirement through its own clause, and the last case of the
  1340	requirement is not needed.
  1341	\end{description}

1714	\subsection{The single-precision floating-point type}
  1715	\seclabel{revival-rr32}
  1716	
  1717	\begin{description}
  1718	\item[Affected sections] \secref{basic-rationals}; \secref{revival-numbers}.
  1719	\item[Change] The passage that names the number types names \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}
  1720	(\STR{RR32}) beside \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, a sibling of the others under
  1721	\TYP{Number}, and says that \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}.
  1722	The effect of \secref{revival-numbers} no longer says that the library's
  1723	\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} stays below \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
  1724	\item[Rationale] \Library\ declared \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} a value object extending
  1725	\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, so that a value of \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} was also a value of
  1726	\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, which \secref{types-libraries} excludes: ``These types are
  1727	mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them.''
  1728	The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) keeps that sentence
  1729	(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
  1730	977--978, in the revival's repository).
  1731	Route~A makes the number types siblings under \TYP{Number}, each with its own
  1732	algebra, and the revival decided on 26~September 2026 that a conversion between
  1733	number types is a coercion where it is exact; every \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} value is
  1734	exact in \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
  1735	\Library\ now declare \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} extending \TYP{Number} and the four
  1736	algebraic traits at its own type, as they declare \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, and
  1737	\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}'s coercion from it
  1738	(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi}, lines 47--48;
  1739	\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi}, lines 291--296).
  1740	The team's own compiler library has declared the two types siblings since its
  1741	change of 31~August 2009, whose message says ``RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64''
  1742	and ``this would be a good time to get coercion working''; it declares the same
  1743	coercion today (\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi},
  1744	lines 433--435 and 475).
  1745	The example of \secref{widening} computes an \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} with an
  1746	\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} by the declaration on \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} after a coercion from
  1747	\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, which is what the library now does.
  1748	The full reasoning is in
  1749	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-rr32-sibling/decision-record.md}
  1750	in the revival's repository.
  1751	\item[Effect] A value of \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} is not a value of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
  1752	Two \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} values combine by the operators declared on
  1753	\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, into an \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}; an \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} combined
  1754	with an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, a floating-point numeral or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} is
  1755	converted to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, and the result is an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}; an
  1756	\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} is converted where an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} is expected.
  1757	A conversion from \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} into \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, which can lose
  1758	precision, stays explicit.
  1759	\item[Original text] The Working Draft of February 2011 names \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}
  1760	in no passage of the number chapters; it says that ``32-bit precision floats are
  1761	written \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}''
  1762	(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/preliminaries/overview.tex}, line 579),
  1763	that the numeric types are mutually exclusive
  1764	(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex}, line 502), and
  1765	gives the example of \secref{widening}
  1766	(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex}, lines
  1767	844--896).
  1768	The passages this change revises are the revival's own text of
  1769	27~September 2026, not the Working Draft's.
  1770	The passage said, in \nolinkurl{Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex}, lines 27--31,
  1771	before this revision:
  1772	\begin{quote}
  1773	The number types of this chapter are
  1774	the integer types \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
  1775	\EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} (\secref{basic-integers}),
  1776	the rational type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}},
  1777	and the floating-point type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (\STR{RR64}).
  1778	\end{quote}
  1779	and, in line 43:
  1780	\begin{quote}
  1781	\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (\STR{RR64}) coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and from integer numerals (\secref{literals}).
  1782	\end{quote}
  1783	The effect of \secref{revival-numbers} said:
  1784	\begin{quote}
  1785	The library's \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} stays below \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, as before, a
  1786	value object that adds no instantiation of its own.
  1787	\end{quote}
  1788	\item[Route C] The same under route~C: the numeric types are mutually exclusive
  1789	whichever rule on instantiations the compiled type checker keeps.
  1790	\end{description}
  1791	
  1792	\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
  1793	\seclabel{revival-notrevised}
  1794	
  1795	No passage that instantiation exclusion or the reorganized numeric types
  1796	contradict is known to be unrevised.
  1797	The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
  1798	infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is written into
  1799	\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
  1800	(\secref{revival-inference}); the passages that chapter leaves unrevised are the
  1801	sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} by which static parameters are inferred
  1802	before the applicability of a declaration is checked and before declarations
  1803	are compared, the implicit bound of \secref{type-param}, and the rule of
  1804	\chapref{overloaded-declarations} on a naked type parameter of bound \TYP{Any},
  1805	which are to be revised with the overloading chapters. The result of an integer raised to a negative power is not yet given (\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-integers}).
  1806	Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
  1807	\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range is
  1808	settled (\secref{revival-inference}): it converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an
  1809	integer numeral does, so the static ranges of \secref{ranges} and the examples
  1810	whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds stand as written.
  1811	Before the number chapters were revised, this section said:
  1812	\begin{quote}
  1813	The number chapters, \chapref{lib:numbers-basic} (whose integers are \secref{basic-integers})
  1814	and \chapref{lib:numbers-advanced}, are not yet revised.
  1815	Their nested tower, in which each integer type is a subtype of the rational
  1816	one above it and each carries its algebra at its own type, and the
  1817	conditional self-extension of \TYP{RationalQuantity}, are refused by
  1818	instantiation exclusion, as the compiled type checker refuses the
  1819	library's nested tower today.
  1820	They will be revised together with the reorganization of the library's
  1821	numeric types that route~A decides, and not before, because a
  1822	specification ahead of its library is as much an open discrepancy as one
  1823	behind it.
  1824	Until then the rule refuses the tower these chapters describe.
  1825	\end{quote}
  1826	
  1827	\subsection{Route C, the alternative not taken}
  1828	\seclabel{revival-routec}
  1829	
  1830	The team's 2012 patent applications (US~8,843,887 and US~8,898,632;
  1831	Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, and Luchangco) relax the rule for a
  1832	self-typed parameterized trait: a type may be a subtype of several of its
  1833	instantiations when they form a chain.
  1834	The revival built that rule whole as an experiment and measured it.
  1835	It closes the unsoundness that instantiation exclusion guards against only
  1836	together with a rule on return types over every level of a chain and a
  1837	change in how a call chooses among generic methods specialised to
  1838	different instantiations: 188 lines of code in five files of the compiled
  1839	type checker and code generator.
  1840	Reversing route~A for route~C would also need a method per level of a
  1841	chain in the code generator, work in the interpreter, a way past a stack
  1842	overflow of the type checker on the self-typing clauses, and seven library
  1843	declarations, besides undoing the reorganization of the library's numeric
  1844	types.
  1845	Route~C rescues none of the \KWD{where}-clause examples of
  1846	\secref{where-clauses} nor the \TYP{Nothing} of \secref{convenience-types},
  1847	each of which places one type below infinitely many instantiations, which
  1848	no chain contains.
  1849	Under route~C the numeric chapters could have kept the nesting of their
  1850	widths, and their original text, quoted in \secref{revival-numbers} and the
  1851	entries after it and kept in the Working Draft of February 2011, is route~C's
  1852	for that nesting; route~C rescues neither the refined number types nor
  1853	\TYP{RationalQuantity} (\secref{revival-numbers}).
  1854	The record of the experiment is
  1855	\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md} in the
  1856	revival's repository.
  1857	\fussy

1550	\subsection{The inference of a call's static arguments}
  1551	\seclabel{revival-inference}
  1552	
  1553	\begin{description}
  1554	\item[Affected sections] \chapref{type-inference}; \secref{ranges};
  1555	\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-ranges}; \secref{revival-notrevised}.
  1556	\item[Change] \chapref{type-inference}, which held a heading and two draft
  1557	notes, states how the static arguments of a call that does not write them are
  1558	inferred, for type parameters and for \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters.
  1559	The declaration is chosen first, as \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses it, a
  1560	declaration with static parameters being applicable to a call if some instance
  1561	of it within its bounds is, and compared on the parameter types it declares.
  1562	Its static arguments are then inferred: a type, \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
  1563	parameter that a parameter type mentions inside another type is fixed by the
  1564	argument, and a type parameter that the return type mentions inside another
  1565	type by the expected type; a type parameter that
  1566	is the whole type of parameters takes the narrowest type that their arguments
  1567	are substitutable for, which for number arguments is the narrowest type into
  1568	which every one of them converts, and otherwise the union of their types; every
  1569	argument is admitted by substitutability, the coercions the instance needs are
  1570	inserted statically, and the converted call dispatches by subtyping.
  1571	A call written by tight juxtaposition, as a method invocation or as an operator
  1572	application, has an expected type in the contexts the chapter lists, a variable
  1573	or field declaration and an assignment to a variable among them, and is
  1574	inferred again without it when its result then converts.
  1575	A numeral whose conversions tie is read as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a
  1576	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value; any other tie among
  1577	declarations applicable only with coercion is a static error.
  1578	The chapter lists what it does not yet describe, the static arguments of a
  1579	\KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator parameter among them, keeps the
  1580	second of the two draft notes, and has three boxes: on the Working Draft, the
  1581	bound it assumes and the passages it leaves to the revision of the overloading
  1582	chapters; on the interpreter; and on a type parameter that only the return
  1583	type mentions and on the \KWD{bool} parameters that neither implementation
  1584	infers.
  1585	The ranges section says that a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
  1586	component converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an integer numeral does, with a
  1587	box.
  1588	The box in \secref{basic-integers} says that a generic call over two different
  1589	integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into by the rule of
  1590	\chapref{type-inference}.
  1591	\secref{revival-notrevised} says that the rule is written and names the passages
  1592	the chapter leaves unrevised, and it and the effect of \secref{revival-ranges}
  1593	say that the question of a \KWD{nat} parameter in a range is settled.
  1594	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A.
  1595	The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that a generic call over two different
  1596	integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into, by a rule
  1597	written into this chapter; on 27~September 2026 that the compiled type checker
  1598	infers static arguments with coercion and keeps the expected type at a call
  1599	written as \EXP{f(x)}, with a retry without it so that a coercion of the result
  1600	still applies, and that the chapter is written with it; and on 28~September
  1601	2026 that a coercion makes a call possible and never changes which declaration
  1602	runs when one is applicable without it, the declaration chosen being then
  1603	instantiated by that rule, that a numeral whose conversions tie is read as a
  1604	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and that a \KWD{nat} parameter used as a value converts to
  1605	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as a numeral does.
  1606	\chapref{multiple-dispatch}, \secref{idn-ref} and \secref{dotted-method-calls}
  1607	said that static arguments are inferred as \chapref{type-inference} describes,
  1608	and it described nothing; once the compiled type checker infers them by a rule
  1609	the text does not state, the text and the implementation disagree, so the
  1610	chapter states the rule that the checker builds, and no more.
  1611	The order, a declaration chosen and then instantiated, is that of
  1612	\secref{resolving-coercion}, read on the parameter types that declarations
  1613	declare, as the type group's paper of 2011 reads a declaration with static
  1614	parameters: it ``is applicable to a type if and only if at least one of its
  1615	instances is'' (\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 396--397, in the
  1616	revival's repository).
  1617	The numeral's default is what the interpreter did before this change, giving
  1618	a numeral the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
  1619	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} that holds its value, \library\ declaring their numeral type
  1620	below \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}; the compiled path, whose library declares its
  1621	numeral type beside \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and excluding it, took one of the
  1622	declarations that a numeral left tied, and not always the same one (row~391 of
  1623	the revival's gap ledger).
  1624	It is also the Java programming language's type for an integer literal.
  1625	The compiled type checker gives a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
  1626	value the type of a numeral, and the interpreter makes it a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
  1627	so an \KWD{int} parameter is read as a \KWD{nat} parameter is; on the Java
  1628	Virtual Machine the length and the indices of an array are 32-bit integers.
  1629	The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) gives the coercion relation,
  1630	the coercion of a generic type and the valid instantiations of a quantified
  1631	type (\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
  1632	938--947, 393--400 and 771--789, in the revival's repository) and never uses
  1633	the word ``infer''; the type group's paper leaves the run-time inference of the
  1634	static arguments of a dispatched declaration ``beyond the scope of this paper''
  1635	(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 118--129).
  1636	The full reasoning is in
  1637	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-inference/decision-record.md}
  1638	in the revival's repository.
  1639	\item[Effect] A generic call over two different integer types, or over a number
  1640	type and a numeral, need not write its static argument, and the interim rule
  1641	of the effect of \secref{revival-numbers} ends.
  1642	A declared type fixes a type parameter that the return type of a call written
  1643	as \EXP{f(x)} mentions inside another type, and a call whose result the
  1644	declared type converts is accepted as before.
  1645	Where the conversions of a numeral tie, the \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} declaration or
  1646	instance is taken; where another argument's conversions tie, the call is a
  1647	static error.
  1648	A \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter may be a component of a range, as in the
  1649	specification's own examples.
  1650	Until the overloading chapters are revised, \chapref{multiple-dispatch} says
  1651	that static parameters are inferred before applicability is checked, and
  1652	\secref{type-param} gives a type parameter without an \KWD{extends} clause the
  1653	bound \TYP{Object}.
  1654	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/inference.tex},
  1655	lines 12--27, which held after the chapter's heading two draft notes:
  1656	\begin{quote}
  1657	This chapter will include the Fortress static type inference mechanism.
  1658	\end{quote}
  1659	and the note that the chapter keeps:
  1660	\begin{quote}
  1661	\begin{itemize}
  1662	\item There seems to be a circular dependency between inference and
  1663	juxtaposition disambiguation -- you have to know if the subexpressions have
  1664	arrow types to disambiguate, but you can't do that without using inference,
  1665	which requires knowing how the variable of unknown type is used.
  1666	\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the
  1667	spec'' on 06/05/07)
  1668	\item Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers
  1669	\TYP{BottomType}s for static parameters?
  1670	\end{itemize}
  1671	\end{quote}
  1672	The other passages this change revises are the revival's own text of 27 and
  1673	28~September 2026, not the Working Draft's.
  1674	The ranges section said, in
  1675	\nolinkurl{Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex}, lines 46--48, before
  1676	this revision:
  1677	\begin{quote}
  1678	An integer numeral converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{literals}), and
  1679	it is a static error if a component of an explicit range has an integer type
  1680	other than \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}.
  1681	\end{quote}
  1682	The box in \secref{basic-integers} ended, in
  1683	\nolinkurl{Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex}, lines 90--94:
  1684	\begin{quote}
  1685	A generic call over two different integer types is to infer the
  1686	narrowest type that both coerce into, by a rule to be written into
  1687	\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation; until then such a
  1688	call writes its static argument, as in
  1689	\EXP{f\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket(a, b)}.
  1690	\end{quote}
  1691	The effect of \secref{revival-ranges} ended:
  1692	\begin{quote}
  1693	Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter may be a component of a range is not settled
  1694	(\secref{revival-notrevised}).
  1695	\end{quote}
  1696	and \secref{revival-notrevised} said:
  1697	\begin{quote}
  1698	The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
  1699	infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is to be written into
  1700	\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
  1701	(\secref{revival-numbers}).
  1702	\end{quote}
  1703	and
  1704	\begin{quote}
  1705	Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
  1706	\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range
  1707	is not settled (\secref{revival-ranges}); the static ranges of
  1708	\secref{ranges} and the examples whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds are
  1709	not revised.
  1710	\end{quote}
  1711	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
  1712	\end{description}
  1713	
  1714	\subsection{The single-precision floating-point type}

1462	\subsection{The example of coercion resolution}
  1463	\seclabel{revival-coercion-example}
  1464	
  1465	\begin{description}
  1466	\item[Affected section] \secref{resolving-coercion}.
  1467	\item[Change] In the example over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
  1468	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} excludes the two others and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
  1469	excludes \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}; the sentence after it names the exclusion and the
  1470	rejection from which \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64 \morespecific \mathbb{Z}128} follows, and
  1471	says that the same facts make the example's two overloadings valid.
  1472	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A. The example contradicted
  1473	the definition before it: \VAR{T} is no less specific than \VAR{U} only if \VAR{T} is
  1474	a subtype of \VAR{U} or excludes, coerces to and rejects \VAR{U}, and without the
  1475	clauses \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} neither excludes \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128} nor rejects it.
  1476	The clauses added are those the definition and the Meet Rule of
  1477	\secref{more-specific-rule} need, spelled as \library\ spell the exclusions of
  1478	their integer types, each type excluding the wider ones
  1479	(\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi}, lines 510--511 and 552--553).
  1480	The team's later Types chapter says the same of an \KWD{excludes} clause: an
  1481	instantiation of the declared trait ``excludes every type in this set''
  1482	(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines 344--351,
  1483	in the revival's repository).
  1484	\item[Effect] The example is a valid program, and both implementations of the revival
  1485	run it as printed, the call resolving to \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}64)}; as the working draft
  1486	printed it, both refuse it.
  1487	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex},
  1488	lines 551--552, the first two lines of the example:
  1489	\begin{quote}
  1490	\begin{Fortress}
  1491	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}32 \KWD{end}\)\\
  1492	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}64\)
  1493	\end{Fortress}
  1494	\end{quote}
  1495	and lines 562--565:
  1496	\begin{quote}
  1497	Then the call \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}32)} resolves to the
  1498	declaration \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}64)} because $\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
  1499	\morespecific \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}$, which follows from the fact that
  1500	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.
  1501	\end{quote}
  1502	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
  1503	\end{description}

   367	
   368	\subsection{The calculi}
   369	\seclabel{revival-calculi}
   370	
   371	\begin{description}
   372	\item[Affected sections] In \appref{calculi}: \basiccore\
   373	(Section~\ref{basic-calculus}), \wherecore\ (\appref{where-calculus}),
   374	\overloadingcore\ (\appref{overloading-calculus}) and \acffdcore\
   375	(Section~\ref{acffd-calculus}).
   376	\item[Change] One box at the opening of each calculus, saying that the
   377	calculus predates instantiation exclusion and naming the shape it admits
   378	that the rule refuses: in \basiccore, an object that extends two different
   379	instantiations of a parameterized trait declaring no method, so that its
   380	statement that all of its valid programs are valid Fortress programs no
   381	longer holds for every program; in \wherecore, a \KWD{where}-clause
   382	variable in a supertype, which its subtyping rule turns into one supertype
   383	for each witness of the variable; in \overloadingcore, the same object as
   384	in \basiccore, which its rule for valid method declarations admits because
   385	the trait declares no method; in \acffdcore, a trait that extends an
   386	instantiation of itself at its parameter's bound, which conditions (2)
   387	and (3) of its rule for an acyclic type hierarchy admit.
   388	The rules of the calculi and their soundness claims are not changed.
   389	\item[Rationale] The calculi are the team's formal record of this working
   390	draft as it stood, and the rule changes the language, not that record.
   391	New premises in their rules would be new formal work, and would reopen
   392	soundness claims that were proved for the rules as they are written.
   393	The revival decided on this treatment on 26~September 2026.
   394	\item[Effect] None on the language or on either implementation.
   395	The four calculi admit programs, in the shapes named, that are not valid
   396	Fortress programs.
   397	\item[Original text] The calculi are unchanged. The statement that the box
   398	in \basiccore\ qualifies is in
   399	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/calculi/basic/calculus.tex},
   400	lines 16--19:
   401	\begin{quote}
   402	Following the precedent set by prior core calculi such as Featherweight
   403	Generic Java~\cite{fgj},
   404	we have abided by the restriction that all valid \basiccore\ programs are
   405	valid Fortress programs.
   406	\end{quote}
   407	The shapes the other three boxes name are admitted by
   408	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/calculi/where/syntax.tex},
   409	lines 82--91, and
   410	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/calculi/where/static.tex},
   411	lines 53--81 and 329--342, by
   412	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/calculi/overloading/static.tex},
   413	lines 52--82, 107--136 and 270--275, and by
   414	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/calculi/acffd/static.tex},
   415	lines 46--88.
   416	Before this entry, \secref{revival-notrevised} said of the calculi:
   417	\begin{quote}
   418	The calculi of \appref{calculi} predate the rule and are not yet revised:
   419	the calculus with \KWD{where} clauses (\appref{where-calculus}) lets a
   420	\KWD{where}-clause variable occur in a supertype, the calculus with an
   421	acyclic type hierarchy admits a trait that extends an instantiation of
   422	itself at its parameter's bound, and the basic calculus states that all of
   423	its valid programs are valid Fortress programs, while it admits an object
   424	that extends two instantiations of a parameterized trait declaring no
   425	method.
   426	How they are to be revised awaits a decision of the revival.
   427	\end{quote}
